glencore-trading-chief-suspended.headline: Glencore suspends iron-ore trading chief amid $2bn Radiant World fraud dispute
glencore-trading-chief-suspended.body_md:
Glencore has suspended Peter Hill, the head of its iron ore trading desk, pending a review of the Swiss commodities giant's dealings with Radiant World, a trading partner it now publicly accuses of fraud. The suspension, first reported by Bloomberg, comes with an uncomfortable detail attached: messages showing Hill instructing a Radiant World counterpart to keep sensitive discussions off email.

"Say nothing on email," Hill wrote in a WhatsApp message to a Radiant World contact in early April 2025, according to Bloomberg, which reviewed the correspondence. Other messages dating back to 2023 show Hill describing Glencore as a key backer of the Radiant World group and suggesting he held effective decision-making authority over aspects of its trading — the kind of informal influence that sits awkwardly next to a company under active regulatory supervision.

![Glencore's headquarters in Baar, Switzerland](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fd/Glencore_Headquarters_in_Baar%2C_Switzerland.jpg)

## From partnership to $2bn lawsuit

Glencore was, until recently, one of Radiant World's most important financial backers. That relationship has now collapsed into a Singapore lawsuit in which Radiant World and an affiliated trader, Sapphire Minmetals, are seeking $2 billion in damages, alleging fraud, breach of contract and conspiracy. Radiant World's claim centres on a 2021 episode in which it says Glencore demanded $1.1 billion in mark-to-market payments, then extracted more than $800 million from the relationship between 2021 and 2026 on the promise of a long-term partnership before cutting ties this year.

Radiant World has gone further, alleging that Glencore deliberately kept the arrangement out of its audited records because of concerns about the US Department of Justice's independent compliance monitors — installed for three years after Glencore's 2022 guilty pleas to foreign bribery and commodity price manipulation, which cost it roughly $700 million in fines, forfeiture and disgorgement in the US alone. Radiant World says the arrangement was made with the knowledge of Glencore's most senior leadership, naming chief executive Gary Nagle, chief financial officer Steve Kalmin and former chief executive Ivan Glasenberg.

Glencore has pushed back hard in the other direction. It says it uncovered evidence that Radiant World and Sapphire Minmetals sent lenders falsified invoices, fabricated contracts and emails purporting to be from Glencore staff. Separately, a Jefferies Financial Group fund has accused the same two companies of falsifying iron ore invoices, prompting a London court to impose a $499 million worldwide freezing order against them.

## Why the emails matter

Hill, who joined Glencore in 2009 after a run of marketing roles at BHP Billiton and built out its iron ore trading franchise, is not a defendant in either lawsuit. But instructions to keep a paper trail off email land badly for a company already operating under a DOJ-appointed monitor tasked with certifying that its controls actually work. Whatever the merits of the fraud claims on either side, evidence that a senior trader sought to suppress written records is the kind of finding compliance monitors and prosecutors weigh independently of who wins the underlying commercial dispute.

Glencore has not disclosed the scope or expected timeline of its internal review, nor commented in detail on Hill's status beyond confirming he has been stood down from his duties.

The Singapore case and the London freezing order both continue, and Glencore's compliance monitorship — a condition of its 2022 settlement — runs for three years from that date, putting continued DOJ scrutiny squarely astride the current dispute. The next marker will be whichever court moves first: a Singapore hearing date on the $2 billion claim, or the outcome of Glencore's own internal review into what its iron ore desk was doing off the record.

shell-lng-buffer-warning.headline: Shell warns shrinking LNG buffers leave global gas market exposed
shell-lng-buffer-warning.body_md:
Shell's latest reckoning of the global LNG market carries a blunt message for anyone budgeting for a cold European winter: the cushion is gone. In prepared remarks around its LNG Outlook update and at Gastech in September, Shell executives put a number on it — roughly 36 million tonnes of Middle Eastern LNG supply, mostly Qatari and Emirati, has been absent from the market so far this year compared with 2025. Only about 20 million tonnes of that has been made good by new US and Canadian cargoes. The rest has come out of demand destruction and drawn-down storage, which is another way of saying the market has been quietly eating its own reserves for months.

![Ras Laffan LNG terminal, Qatar](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Ras_Laffan_LNG_terminal_in_2012.jpg)

> **In one sentence:** Shell says roughly 36 million tonnes of lost LNG capacity is exhausting spare market buffers, a warning with direct implications for European winter gas prices.

## Where the tonnes went

The hole traces back to March, when Iranian missiles struck Ras Laffan Industrial City, the sprawling complex 80km north of Doha that handles close to a fifth of the world's LNG trade. The strikes disabled Trains 4 and 6, wiping out about 12.8 million tonnes a year of capacity — roughly 17% of Qatar's export base — and also knocked out Shell's Pearl gas-to-liquids plant on the same site. Qatar's south production area, hit hardest, saw capacity cut from 36 million tonnes annually to 24 million. Wood Mackenzie has said a meaningful share of that lost capacity won't return for years, since replacement gas turbines carry lead times of two to four years. Two of three trains at the older Qatargas-1 site have since been restarted, but full recovery still hinges on stable transit through the Strait of Hormuz, which has not returned to pre-war shipping patterns even with a ceasefire nominally in place.

Shell's Peter Clarke counterpart at ExxonMobil made the same distinction Shell has been drawing all year: reopening the strait to traffic is not the same as restoring the trade flows that existed before it closed. Buyers who redirected long-term contracts elsewhere, insurers who repriced war risk, and shipowners who rerouted tonnage do not simply snap back once the missiles stop. Cederic Cremers, Shell's president of integrated gas, described the episode as "a system-wide shock with disruption cascading across all segments of the economy," while allowing that the LNG industry had "proved resilient." He was notably less sanguine on price, telling reporters flatly that "the prices are too high right now" — an unusual admission from a seller.

## Why the buffer matters more than the shortfall

The 36-million-tonne figure alone doesn't explain the alarm; global LNG trade runs to roughly 400 million tonnes a year, so the absolute loss is a manageable single-digit percentage. What has Shell and its peers exercised is the depletion of the slack that normally exists to absorb a shock like this one. Spot cargoes that once floated between Asian and European buyers depending on price have been drawn down. Storage that would typically be topped up over summer has instead been used to plug the Qatari gap. The International Energy Forum has estimated spare liquefaction capacity fell around 14 billion cubic metres short of the volumes that would normally have moved through Hormuz in 2025 — a buffer that, in a calmer year, gives the market room to shrug off a terminal outage or a cold snap. That room has largely disappeared.

Europe enters the October-to-March heating season with storage at about 67–68% of capacity, against a five-year seasonal average near 88% and short of the EU's own 80%-by-December target — a shortfall put at somewhere between 14 and 20 billion cubic metres with, as one analyst note put it, no injection-season buffer left to draw on. Dutch TTF, the European benchmark, has been trading near €80/MWh in mid-September, having touched roughly €84 earlier in the month — levels last seen consistently during the 2022 crisis. Analysts at Morgan Stanley have sketched a base case near €85/MWh for the winter, a bear case near €50 if Qatari flows normalise by late November into a mild season, and a bull case as high as €210 if they do not and the winter turns cold. Wood Mackenzie's Simon Flowers summarised the asymmetry: "There's a big risk if we have a cold winter because there's very little spare supply available."

![LNG tanker Christophe de Margerie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/90/LNG_tanker_Christophe_de_Margerie.jpg)

## The read-through for markets

For traders, the mechanism is straightforward even if the outcome isn't: thin buffers convert ordinary variance — a colder week in Germany, a delayed cargo, a fresh incident near Hormuz — into outsized price moves, because there is no longer a comfortable margin of spare supply to absorb the surprise. That is a different risk profile from 2022's crisis, which was driven by the sudden loss of Russian pipeline gas; this one is layered on top of an already-tight Asian market and a shipping lane still shadowed by the Iran conflict, whose ceasefire has continued to fray past the 200-day mark. Energy volatility of this kind tends not to stay contained to gas contracts. It feeds directly into European industrial input costs, headline inflation prints, and — as the Bank of England's own split verdict on rates this month showed — central bank calculations already complicated by elevated gilt yields.

The next real test arrives with the first sustained cold snap, whenever it comes. Watch European storage withdrawal rates against the seasonal norm, and watch whether Qatar's south-site trains come back online ahead of Wood Mackenzie's multi-year timeline. Until either buffer — storage or Qatari capacity — visibly rebuilds, Shell's warning stands: the market has little room left to absorb another shock.

revolut-dual-listing.headline: Revolut weighs dual London/New York stock listing, CEO confirms
revolut-dual-listing.body_md:
Nik Storonsky has spent the better part of two years telling anyone who would listen that London's stock market cannot compete with New York. On Wednesday, in an interview with the French newspaper Les Echos, Revolut's founder and chief executive softened that stance just enough to matter: the $115 billion fintech, he said, is now weighing a dual listing on both the London Stock Exchange and New York's Nasdaq.

It is the first time Storonsky has put a London leg on the table at all. As recently as 2024 he dismissed the idea outright, arguing the UK market lacked the depth of buyers to support a float of Revolut's size. The reversal matters less as a concession to London boosters than as a signal of how mega-valued European fintechs are starting to think about going public — not as an either/or between home market and Wall Street, but as a sequencing question.

![Nik Storonsky, founder and CEO of Revolut, speaking on stage at Web Summit](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/63/Nikolay_Storonsky.jpg)

## Why New York still wins the argument

Storonsky was characteristically blunt about where his preference lies. "It's a larger market," he told Les Echos. "It includes institutional investors, hedge funds, fund managers and a considerable number of individual investors." The calculus, as he framed it, is simple: "We have the choice between selling in a small market with few buyers, or in a gigantic market with a huge number of buyers who will compete fiercely for our shares. Therefore, yes, we prefer the United States."

That logic tracks the valuation trajectory. Revolut priced a secondary share sale in July at $115 billion — shares changing hands at $2,017 apiece, a jump of more than 50% from the $75 billion mark set less than a year earlier. The Financial Times has reported internal discussions of an eventual IPO valuation as high as $150 billion to $200 billion. At those numbers, a London listing alone would install Revolut among Britain's largest public companies, ahead of Barclays and NatWest by market capitalisation and within range of BP — a fact London Stock Exchange officials have not been shy about pointing out as they court the company.

![The London Stock Exchange building at Paternoster Square](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c6/London_Stock_Exchange%2C_Paternoster_Square.jpg)

## Building the regulatory scaffolding for two markets

A dual listing requires more than an ambivalent CEO — it requires banking infrastructure on both sides of the Atlantic, and Revolut has spent 2026 assembling exactly that. The company secured a full UK banking licence in March, ending a wait that began with a restricted licence back in 2024, and has picked up additional charters in France, Lithuania, Australia, Colombia and Mexico. In the US it holds conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national bank charter — the missing piece that would let it operate as a full-fledged deposit-taking bank rather than a payments app when it eventually courts American public-market investors.

The underlying business has kept pace. Revenue rose 46% last year to $6 billion, with net profit reaching $1.7 billion, while the customer base grew by more than 16 million to 68.3 million. Those are the kind of growth-plus-profitability numbers that let a company dictate listing venue rather than beg for one — a leverage previous-generation fintechs, many of which went public loss-making or scaled back valuations before their US debuts, rarely had.

None of this means a float is imminent. Storonsky said as recently as April that an IPO was still roughly two years out, and has previously ruled out going public before 2028. The dual-listing idea, for now, is a stated preference rather than a filed prospectus, and market conditions — rates, risk appetite, the state of tech valuations generally — will do as much to set the timeline as anything happening inside Revolut's Canary Wharf headquarters.

## What a dual listing would signal for the sector

What has shifted is the framing. A decade of European fintechs — Wise chief among them — treated a US listing as the default aspiration and a domestic one as a consolation prize, if they considered it at all. Wise itself flipped that script in 2025 by shifting its primary listing to New York while retaining London ties, a move Revolut's dual-track thinking now echoes from the other direction. If Revolut follows through, it would test whether a single company can genuinely serve two exchanges' worth of liquidity, disclosure regimes and index inclusion — Nasdaq-100 ambitions on one side, an FTSE 100 weighting on the other — without either market treating it as an afterthought.

The next marker to watch is not a listing date but a venue decision: whether Revolut treats London and New York as equal primary listings or structures one as a secondary shell, and whether UK regulators offer further sweeteners — on stamp duty, dual-class share rules, or index eligibility — to keep the London leg meaningful rather than symbolic.

nike-arnault-board.headline: Nike adds LVMH heir Alexandre Arnault to board after $200bn market-cap slide
nike-arnault-board.body_md:
Nike has added Alexandre Arnault, the 34-year-old son of LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, to its board of directors — a move that lands eight days after the sportswear giant was dropped from the S&P 100 index of America's largest blue-chip companies.

The appointment, announced September 17, expands Nike's board to twelve members. Arnault currently serves as deputy chief executive of Moët Hennessy, LVMH's wines and spirits arm, a post he has held since early 2025. Before that he spent four years running product, communications and industrial strategy at Tiffany & Co. — where he helped broker a streetwear collaboration with, of all companies, Nike — and four years as chief executive of the German luggage maker Rimowa, where he pushed collaborations with Supreme and Off-White. He also sits on LVMH's own board and is a trustee of New York's Museum of Modern Art.

"His experience across innovation, digital transformation and brand building will be an asset," Nike chief executive Elliott Hill said in a statement announcing the appointment.

## A board seat against a $200bn backdrop

The timing is not incidental. Nike's stock has fallen from a November 2021 peak near $177 to roughly $36 this week, a decline of almost 80% that has erased more than $200bn in market capitalization — from a peak value near $290bn to about $54bn today. That slide dragged Nike out of the S&P 100 on September 21, ending an 18-year run in the index of the market's hundred largest companies. Nike remains in the broader S&P 500.

The underlying business has been sliding in parallel. Fiscal 2026 revenue came in at $46.4 billion, down 2% on a currency-neutral basis, with fourth-quarter Nike Direct sales off 7% and digital sales down 12%. The company has spent much of the year trying to claw back control of its own distribution, pulling online-sales rights from wholesale partners it had leaned on during the pandemic boom, while contending with eight straight quarters of falling sales in China.

![Alexandre Arnault](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/83/Alexandre_Arnault_%C3%A0_l%27universit%C3%A9_Oxford_le_12_juillet_2022.jpg)

David Swartz, an analyst at Morningstar, told Fortune that Nike would not make a board move like this without expecting a tangible payoff, though he noted the arrangement could just as easily be read as a finishing-school posting for Arnault ahead of a bigger role at LVMH someday. Either reading points to the same underlying fact: a company built on performance footwear and marketing muscle is now borrowing credibility from a conglomerate whose luxury labels have weathered the same consumer pullback far better than Nike's own.

The next marker is Nike's fiscal first-quarter earnings, due in early October, which will show whether Hill's turnaround — tighter inventory, direct-distribution clawback, a renewed push in China — is bending the sales trend before the holiday quarter.

british-steel-bailout-costs.headline: Watchdog says ministers lack credible plan as British Steel rescue costs soar
british-steel-bailout-costs.body_md:
Britain is now spending £1.3 million of public money every day keeping British Steel's furnaces lit, and Parliament's spending watchdog says ministers still cannot say when — or whether — that will stop.

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has found that the Department for Business and Trade has no credible plan to return British Steel to a sustainable footing, more than a year after the government took emergency control of the Scunthorpe plant to stop its Chinese owner, Jingye Group, shutting it down. By mid-June, £555m of taxpayer money had already gone into wages and raw materials. The PAC's own projection puts the total bill at up to £1.5bn by 2028 — a figure ministers have not disputed, but have also not budgeted for in any published form.

"British Steel is unable to wash its own face, and government is now in charge," said Clive Betts, the committee's deputy chair. "Having brought British Steel onto the taxpayers' books, it is now up to government to explain its plan." The committee's report is blunter still: officials could not give MPs "even indicative estimates" of the final cost or the timeline for reaching one, and taxpayers "remain exposed to significant and growing costs and uncertainty — it is not clear whether the money will ever be recovered."

![Blast furnaces at Scunthorpe Steelworks](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e1/Blast_furnaces_at_Scunthorpe_Steelworks_-_geograph.org.uk_-_5844975.jpg)

## No route back to private hands

The emergency intervention in April 2025 was framed as a rescue, not a takeover — but British Steel was formally nationalised on 16 July 2026, some 15 months after ministers first floated the idea. Jingye, for its part, argues it is owed roughly £1bn in compensation and has begun proceedings to recover it; Beijing has called the nationalisation "strongly dissatisfying." The government has since gone further, nationalising Speciality Steel UK and its 1,300 jobs in mid-September — extending the same open-ended exposure to a second site just as the PAC was publishing its verdict on the first.

What the committee wants is unglamorous but specific: a published plan setting out the intended production model, a decarbonisation pathway for the plant's ageing blast furnaces, a route to financial sustainability, and a costed timetable showing where the money comes from and when it stops. None of that exists yet in public form.

For a government already fielding pressure over gilt yields sitting near three-decade highs and a fractious Bank of England vote, an open-ended industrial commitment with no defined exit is not a reassuring signal to bond markets watching how the Treasury handles contingent liabilities. The next marker is the government's formal response to the PAC report, due within two months under standard select committee procedure — and whether it contains a number ministers are willing to be held to.

airbus-regional-jet-grounded.headline: Airbus's regional-jet venture grounds planes over toxic-fume complaints
airbus-regional-jet-grounded.body_md:
Air Corsica, the airline that connects Corsica to mainland France, has pulled four of its seven ATR 72-600 turboprops from service after pilots repeatedly reported fumes leaking into the cockpit and cabin — some crew members describing migraines after exposure. The Wall Street Journal reports that ATR, the aircraft's manufacturer, and Pratt & Whitney, which builds its engines, are now investigating, with one grounded aircraft sent to ATR's Toulouse facility for testing.

The episode is small in scale but awkward in ownership. ATR is a 50-50 joint venture between Airbus and Italy's Leonardo, and the aircraft in question use the PW127XT, a newer Pratt & Whitney Canada engine that became the default option on ATR deliveries after Air Corsica took the type's first unit in 2022. The same engine has since been ordered by FedEx and IndiGo, which is the detail that matters most for anyone pricing this as an isolated glitch versus a design flaw: if investigators trace the fumes to the engine itself rather than a maintenance lapse or a one-off contamination event, the finding travels well beyond a Corsican regional carrier's fleet of 14 aircraft.

![ATR 72-600 in Air Corsica livery, photographed at Nice airport](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/54/F-HXKE_%40_NCE%2C_2024-01-18.jpg)

## What's leaking, and why it's familiar

The mechanism under scrutiny is a so-called fume event: engine oil seeping past worn seals and vaporizing into the bleed air that most commercial aircraft — turboprops and jets alike — draw from the engine to pressurize the cabin. Air Corsica says no causal link has yet been confirmed between the reported "technical events" and any specific fault, and that it is working with ATR and its equipment partners to isolate the source. ATR maintains the aircraft meet regulatory safety standards; Pratt & Whitney and Airbus have both declined to comment.

The timing works against generous interpretation. A broader Journal investigation published earlier this year found fume-event reports climbing sharply across the industry — a combined 660% rise for JetBlue and Spirit between 2016 and 2024 — concentrated on aircraft using bleed-air designs, with occupational studies linking the leaked vapors to neurotoxic compounds such as tricresyl phosphate. The FAA's 2024 reauthorization now mandates better fume-event reporting and crew training, a regulatory backdrop that leaves little room for manufacturers to wave off individual incidents as noise.

## The cost of grounding four turboprops

For now this reads as operational rather than financial. Air Corsica has chartered replacement capacity — an Airbus A319 from Amelia, an A350 from Air Caraïbes, and an extra ATR from Chalair — to cover more than 100 substitute flights through the end of October and preserve the public-service routes linking Corsica to Paris, Marseille, Nice and Lyon. One of the grounded aircraft had also been chartered by Airbus itself for inter-factory shuttle flights, forcing a swap there too.

The real exposure sits with the investigation's outcome. A contamination finding closes the story quickly; a design finding reopens questions about ATR's standing in a regional-jet and turboprop market it already shares uneasily with Embraer, and about how much scrutiny Pratt & Whitney's engine family — already dealing with unrelated delivery bottlenecks flagged by Airbus — can absorb before it dents order confidence at FedEx and IndiGo. ATR's Toulouse test results, and any EASA response, are the next things worth watching.

boeing-cash-flow-delay.headline: Boeing's $10bn free cash flow target pushed out further as 737 Max ramp-up slips
boeing-cash-flow-delay.body_md:
Boeing's chief executive has, for the third time in as many quarters, told investors that the company's road back to durable profitability runs a little longer than previously advertised. Speaking at Morgan Stanley's Laguna Conference on 16 September, Kelly Ortberg said stabilising 737 Max production at the target rate of 47 jets a month is taking "a little bit longer" than planned — and with it, Boeing's long-standing goal of $10bn in annual free cash flow slides further over the horizon.

"We are not stable yet at 47 a month," Ortberg told the conference. "We just have not seen the flow improvements that we expected in the time frame." The admission cost Boeing shares roughly 2.5% on the day, extending a slide that has left the stock down more than 10% over the trailing month and trading near $202, well below its 200-day average of $220.

![Boeing 737 Max rolls out of the Renton, Washington factory](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Boeing_737_MAX_%2823514088802%29.jpg)

## Wings, not fuselages, are the holdup

The bottleneck, Ortberg said, sits at Boeing's Renton, Washington plant, where wings for the Max are built before being shipped to the Everett line for final assembly. The FAA capped Max output at 38 a month in the wake of the 2024 door-plug blowout on an Alaska Airlines jet; clearing that ceiling to 47, and eventually 52, was meant to be largely a matter of discipline and time. Instead, wing-flow rates have lagged the recovery plan Boeing laid out to regulators and investors, and hitting 52 a month next year will now require both a fix at Renton and FAA certification of a second Max line in Everett.

There was a rare bright spot: the FAA certified the smallest variant, the 737 Max 7, in August, and Ortberg said certification of the largest, the Max 10 — which accounts for roughly 30% of all Max orders and is running years behind its original schedule — is coming "very soon." Boeing is already building two Max 10s in Everett ahead of that sign-off.

## The cash flow math gets pushed out again

The production slip flows straight through to the balance sheet. Boeing's 2026 guidance had pointed to $1bn-$3bn in free cash flow, with $3bn treated as the upside case; the company now expects to land closer to $2bn, the midpoint, as slower 737 output compounds with delays ramping the 787 Dreamliner to 10 jets a month — itself held back by engine shortages. The 787 line, held up as the model for how the Max ramp should eventually look, is stabilised at 8 a month but has yet to move higher.

Management still calls the long-term $10bn annual free cash flow target "very attainable," and points to a second-quarter print of $631m — Boeing's first meaningful positive free cash flow quarter in years — as evidence the underlying trajectory is real. But each slip in the production timeline pushes that $10bn goalpost further out, and with the 10-year Treasury yield sitting near 5%, the present value of cash promised in 2028 or 2029 is worth markedly less than cash promised in 2026. That arithmetic, as much as the delay itself, is what moved the stock.

## Why the pattern matters more than the delay

A single missed month on a factory floor is not, on its own, remarkable for an aircraft maker still working through the aftermath of the Max's 2019-2020 grounding and the 2024 quality crisis. What is harder to wave away is the repetition: Boeing has now pushed back its cash-generation timeline enough times that investors are pricing in a structural gap between what management projects and what the factory floor delivers. Ortberg was hired in 2024 in part to close that gap and rebuild credibility with regulators, airlines and shareholders alike. Wing production at Renton was flagged as a fixable, mechanical problem — not a redesign of the jet or a supplier crisis — which makes the miss more a story about execution than about engineering.

Boeing carries a record backlog of $715bn, including $597bn in commercial orders across more than 6,200 aircraft, so demand is not the constraint. The constraint is Boeing's own ability to convert a factory back to full health years after grounding it. Watch the Max 10 certification decision, expected imminently, and the next quarterly cash flow print for whether the Renton wing line has actually turned the corner — or whether the $10bn target quietly slips again.

tempus-ai-rally.headline: Tempus AI shares extend rally after Morgan Stanley lifts revenue outlook
tempus-ai-rally.body_md:
Tempus AI's stock has climbed roughly 30% over the past week, closing Thursday at $79.65 after a 13.8% single-session jump, following upbeat commentary from Morgan Stanley on the healthcare-AI company's reimbursement outlook. The move is large by any measure — but it says more about how thin the market's information set is on this stock than about any transformation at the company itself.

The catalyst was a Morgan Stanley Global Healthcare Conference appearance on September 15, where Tempus executives, including founder and chief executive Eric Lefkofsky, laid out the case for two of the firm's diagnostic products getting materially better reimbursement terms than the market had priced in. Lefkofsky said clearer pricing on the company's xT genomic sequencing test could add $80 million to $100 million in annual revenue, while newly clarified approval and pricing on its xF liquid-biopsy test could contribute another $250 million to $300 million. Combined, Morgan Stanley put the potential uplift at $330 million to $400 million a year — a meaningful add-on for a company that guided to roughly $1.6 billion in full-year revenue.

## What actually changed

It's worth being precise about what did and didn't happen here. Tempus did not announce a new product, a new partnership, or a beat against consensus estimates that day — the rally followed prepared remarks and analyst framing, not a press release or an SEC filing with new financial detail. What changed is that Morgan Stanley — and by extension the sell-side consensus that leans on it — now has more clarity on reimbursement mechanics that were previously uncertain, and revised its model accordingly. Consensus forward EPS estimates have moved from roughly -$0.11 to a fraction of a cent positive over the past 90 days, with eight upward analyst revisions in the past month, according to data compiled by 24/7 Wall St.

The underlying business has also been running hot on its own terms. Tempus's most recent quarter showed revenue of $382.5 million, up 21.6% year-on-year, with oncology test volumes accelerating 31%. Lefkofsky told investors the company's data-licensing arm — which sells de-identified clinical and genomic data to drugmakers — booked roughly $200 million in the second quarter from clients including AstraZeneca, GSK and Merck, and said management now expects to exceed its own multiyear 25% growth target. Full-year guidance was lifted to $1.595–1.605 billion in revenue with adjusted EBITDA near $65 million.

## The gap between the stock move and the reporting

Even after the rally, the stock trades below its 52-week high of $104.32, and the average analyst price target of $68.18 now sits well under Thursday's close — meaning the rally has outrun the models built to justify it, at least until those targets are revised upward, which several desks are already doing. At roughly 9 times sales, Tempus is priced as a growth story, not a diagnostics company with a conventional earnings multiple.

That combination — a single conference appearance, a sell-side reframing, and a 30% weekly move — is a reminder of how much of the current AI-adjacent healthcare trade rests on narrow, analyst-mediated information flows rather than independently verified data. Morgan Stanley's numbers come from company guidance relayed at an investor conference; they have not yet shown up in a 10-Q. Nothing here is disqualifying, but it is a distinction between an analyst upgrade and a demonstrated change in the addressable market for healthcare AI diagnostics, which remains as opaque as it was a week ago.

## What comes next

The next real test is Tempus's third-quarter print, whenever it lands, which will show whether the xT and xF reimbursement gains Lefkofsky described are showing up in booked revenue rather than guidance language. Until then, the stock's next moves are likely to track further sell-side price-target revisions rather than new operating data — a pattern common to single-stock rallies built on a conference appearance rather than a filing.

fluence-energy-guidance-cut.headline: Fluence Energy stock plunges after guidance cut raises production concerns
fluence-energy-guidance-cut.body_md:
Shares in Fluence Energy fell roughly 22% on Thursday after the grid-scale battery storage maker slashed its full-year revenue and profit outlook for the second time in 2026, pointing to a manufacturing ramp-up that has gone badly wrong at its Houston plant. The stock closed near $7, deep into 52-week-low territory and a fraction of the $33.51 it touched a year ago.

> "Our team underestimated the complexity of the ramp-up of the Houston facility, specifically the major issues that have emerged."

That admission, from chief executive Julian Nebreda, understates the scale of the miss. The Houston site — which makes thermal-management enclosures central to Fluence's battery systems — was supposed to be turning out eleven units a day by late summer as part of the company's push toward US-made content. Instead it managed less than one a day in August, undone by an underperforming automated welding line and a shortage of skilled labor. Output has since recovered to about three units daily, still a fraction of plan.

![Grid-scale battery storage installation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c6/Tesvolt_battery_energy_storage_system_Rheineck.jpg)

## The numbers behind the drop

Fluence now expects fiscal 2026 revenue of about $2.4 billion, down from roughly $3 billion guided just last month — a $600 million write-down in a single quarter. Adjusted EBITDA guidance swung from a loss of about $10 million to a loss of about $200 million. Management attributed roughly 80% of the shortfall to US production problems: $450 million from the Houston delays themselves, another $65 million in late-delivery penalties owed to customers, and $85 million in added logistics costs from working around the bottleneck.

The order backlog, by contrast, remains large — $6.4 billion by the company's own count — which is precisely what has unnerved analysts rather than reassured them. Barclays cut Fluence to Underweight from Equal Weight and dropped its price target to $10 from $16, citing a widening gap between paper backlog and the company's ability to actually deliver and bill for it, alongside rising capital needs and thinning liquidity. Baird went further, cutting its target by 70% to $3 and downgrading to Underperform. Fluence has appointed a new chief operating officer, Bernard Dasant, to take charge of manufacturing and supply-chain execution, and has said it does not expect to need additional capital in fiscal 2027.

## A bellwether problem, not just a Fluence problem

Fluence is not a niche supplier. As one of the largest makers of grid-scale battery systems, backed by Siemens and AES, it has functioned as something close to a proxy for the health of the storage build-out that utilities are counting on to firm up solar and wind generation and to backstop the surge in power demand from data centers. A single company's welding line does not, on its own, prove an industry-wide ceiling. But the specifics here are the kind that recur across capital-intensive manufacturing ramps: automation that does not scale as modeled, and not enough trained labor to make up the difference by hand. Those are structural constraints, not one-off accidents, and they are exactly the ones that show up whenever a sector tries to reshore fast to capture domestic-content incentives.

CFO Ahmed Pasha added a wrinkle worth watching: some data-center developers may now choose to forgo US tax credits altogether in favor of faster delivery from non-domestic supply chains — a sign that speed-to-power is starting to outweigh the incentive math for at least some buyers, which would cut against the very reshoring push Fluence's Houston plant was built to serve.

The next checkpoint is Fluence's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call, when investors will look for evidence that the Houston line's output run-rate is climbing toward its original eleven-a-day target rather than plateauing near three. Until then, the backlog stays a promise rather than a number on the income statement.

huntington-bancshares-tumble.headline: Huntington Bancshares shares tumble on cut NII and 2027 EPS outlook
huntington-bancshares-tumble.body_md:
Huntington Bancshares shares fell 5.6% on Wednesday, closing at $15.82 after the Columbus, Ohio-based lender told investors at the Barclays Global Financial Services Conference that its earnings trajectory through 2027 will be flatter than promised. Roughly 77.5 million shares changed hands, well above normal volume, as the market repriced a stock that had leaned heavily on a bullish post-merger growth story.

Management cut its 2027 earnings-per-share target to a range of $1.75 to $1.83, down from the $1.90 to $1.93 it had guided to in the spring. It also trimmed 2026 net interest income growth to roughly 35%, from a prior 39–43% range, and cut projected 2026 revenue growth to about 34% from 37%. Those percentages look enormous next to typical bank guidance because they are: Huntington closed its $8.3 billion acquisition of Cadence Bank in February and folded in Texas lender Veritex Holdings last October, so the underlying base is still absorbing two large deals. The cuts describe how much of that combined growth is now expected to show up in the numbers — and it's less than advertised.

## Deposit costs outrunning the model

The culprit is pricing, not credit. Chairman and CEO Steve Steinour told the conference the environment "is materially different and more challenging than we had anticipated at the beginning of the year," adding: "We got caught with a different expectation in the interest-rate environment and the competitive dynamic." Short-term rates have stayed higher for longer than Huntington modeled, and deposit costs have followed: total deposit costs rose roughly 30 basis points between January and August, while the rate paid on interest-bearing deposits reached 2.29% in the second quarter, up 8 basis points sequentially. Net interest margin slipped 3 basis points on the quarter to 3.21%, even after Huntington's prime rate moved to 7.00% following the Federal Reserve's rate increase.

CFO Zach Wasserman pointed to a second front: loan competition. He cited "meaningful acceleration in terms of the competitive environment in indirect auto" that pushed Huntington to pull back originations — auto balances fell 4.3% in the first half of the year — while commercial real estate loans shrank $800 million in the second quarter as borrowers refinanced away faster than expected. Steinour was explicit that the response won't be to chase volume: "What we won't do is change our credit discipline, and we're going to be very disciplined about our risk-adjusted returns." Management still points to a 2027 return on equity above 17%.

![Huntington Center in Columbus, Ohio, where Huntington Bancshares is headquartered](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ab/Columbus_Huntington_Center.jpg)

Some analysts read the reset as overdue rather than alarming — Keefe, Bruyette & Woods described it as a potential "clearing event" that removes an overhang investors had already priced in after BofA downgraded the stock earlier this year on similar concerns. Huntington's shares now trade around 8.8 times the midpoint of its new 2027 EPS estimate, a discount that will either look cheap or prove sticky depending on what regional-bank peers say about deposit competition when they report third-quarter results in mid-October — the next real test of whether this is a Huntington problem or a sector one.

tom-watson-palantir.headline: Tom Watson, former Labour deputy leader, joins Palantir
tom-watson-palantir.body_md:
Tom Watson spent four decades in Labour politics building a reputation as the party's chief fixer — the man who helped topple Tony Blair, steadied Jeremy Corbyn's front bench as deputy leader, and later became a vocal critic of Silicon Valley's grip on public life. On Wednesday he became a senior vice-president at Palantir Technologies, the US data-analytics firm whose UK subsidiary is fighting to keep hold of a £330m NHS contract that ministers are actively reconsidering.

![Official portrait of Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fd/Official_portrait_of_Lord_Watson_of_Wyre_Forest_crop_2.jpg)

Watson, now Lord Watson of Wyre Forest, will work alongside Louis Mosley, Palantir's UK and Europe chief executive, on what the company describes as deepening "the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills." He has taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and given up his parliamentary pass — a formal break from frontline politics, though not from the parts of the state Palantir most wants to sell into.

"Terrifically excited" was how Watson described the move, saying he wanted to help the firm speed up NHS diagnosis, treatment and hospital discharge, and to help "our police to crack crimes and root out corruption." Palantir's chief executive, Alex Karp, framed it as continuity rather than conversion: "This is just the latest chapter of Tom's forty-year fight for better public services. We are fortunate to have him guide us as we help the British government to deliver for the British public."

## A contract under active review

The appointment lands in the middle of the tensest period yet for Palantir's UK public-sector business. The company holds the £330m contract to run the NHS Federated Data Platform, signed in 2023 and due to run to early 2027, with a break clause that has turned the second half of this year into a genuine decision point. Nearly a third of the 16 NHS trusts using the platform are carrying out fewer procedures than before it went live, according to figures compiled by campaign group Foxglove — though one trust, Chelsea and Westminster, accounts for 84% of that fall on its own. Palantir points instead to 110,078 additional hospital procedures it says the platform has enabled since rollout.

The scrutiny goes beyond performance data. The Financial Times has reported that NHS England allowed Palantir staff "unlimited" access to patient records, and the National Data Guardian, Dr Nicola Byrne, pushed NHS England into admitting this summer that its own data protection assessment had wrongly stated that only NHS staff could see identifiable patient data on the system. NHS England has since commissioned Imperial College Projects to run a £700,000 independent evaluation of whether the platform delivers value for money. Separately, Palantir is in court proceedings with London mayor Sadiq Khan over a blocked £50m Metropolitan Police AI contract.

## The access question

Watson is not the first senior political or security figure to land at Palantir's door — former MI6 chief Sir John Sawers and ex-Ministry of Defence strategy director Polly Scully both hold advisory roles there, and Watson himself has been a paid member of the company's Public Services Advisory Board since 2024, disclosed in the House of Lords register of interests. The pattern fits a company that, according to reporting on its UK operations, has spent heavily on securing political access: think-tank donations, Davos receptions, and advisory seats for former officials with standing relationships across Whitehall.

Whether that access converts into contract survival is a separate question from whether it should. A former deputy leader of the governing party's own tradition, arguing publicly for the NHS platform's value at the exact moment officials are deciding whether to trigger its 2027 extension, is either a coincidence of timing or the whole point of the hire. Palantir did not frame it as the latter. The optics do the arguing anyway.

## What's next

The practical test comes at the Department of Health and Social Care's extension decision ahead of the March 2027 break clause, with the Imperial College Projects evaluation due to feed into that call. Until then, expect Watson and Mosley to be the public faces defending a contract that Foxglove, the National Data Guardian and a chunk of NHS trusts have already made politically expensive.

gundlach-zero-ai-exposure.headline: DoubleLine's Gundlach says he holds zero exposure to 'AI epicenter' stocks
gundlach-zero-ai-exposure.body_md:
Jeffrey Gundlach, the DoubleLine Capital founder whose bond-market calls have earned him the nickname "Bond King," says his own portfolio holds none of the stocks driving this year's market gains. Asked about his exposure to the handful of companies powering the artificial-intelligence trade, Gundlach's answer was blunt: virtually zero.

Speaking on The Julia La Roche Show, Gundlach described wanting to be "out of the epicenter" of the AI race. His equity allocation — 30% of his overall portfolio — sits entirely in an equal-weight index of roughly 440 of the highest-revenue companies in the market, rather than the cap-weighted benchmarks where a handful of AI-linked mega-caps now dominate. "We're already close enough to that tipping point that I'd rather step away from the epicenter," he said.

## Why the aversion

Gundlach's case rests on two legs. The first is valuation: he pointed to the S&P 500's Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which he put above 42. Historically, he noted, whenever that measure has exceeded 35, real returns over the following decade have been negative — commonly by around 5% a year after inflation.

The second is credit. Gundlach has been tracking newly issued bonds from AI-linked borrowers and says the stress shows up almost immediately. "The spread starts to blow out," he said, sometimes within days or weeks of issuance — a signal, in his view, that bond investors are pricing risks equity markets have not yet absorbed. Debt markets have historically led equity markets in flagging credit problems, and Gundlach has argued that a diversified mix of investment-grade corporate bonds offers less protection from an AI-driven pullback than most investors assume.

He has also taken aim at the financing structures underpinning the AI buildout. Referring to Nvidia's push to mobilize more than $500 billion in AI infrastructure financing with a group of banks, Gundlach compared the arrangement to issuing 30-year asset-backed securities against warehouses of "newly engineered bananas of unknown life" — his shorthand for financial engineering dressed up with favorable credit ratings. He argues that AI and hyperscale cloud firms are chasing addressable markets that would amount to roughly a quarter of global GDP, calling that "a scenario that simply cannot hold up."

## The trade he's making instead

Rather than shorting AI names outright, Gundlach has rotated into equal-weight equity exposure, shorter-duration corporate bonds, utilities, gold, and local-currency emerging-market debt. He has previously urged investors to hold around 20% of a portfolio in cash, describing the broader market as one of the least healthy of his career. Technology now accounts for roughly 40% of the S&P 500 by his estimate, which is precisely the concentration his equal-weight approach is built to avoid — the same handful of names that pushed the index higher this year could just as easily drag it down together.

Gundlach separately criticized the Federal Reserve's latest quarter-point rate cut as insufficient given the central bank's own forecast that inflation won't return to 2% until 2029, calling monetary policy "behind the curve."

## What it doesn't prove

One manager's zero weighting is not a market call that AI stocks are about to fall — DoubleLine is fundamentally a bond shop, and Gundlach has flagged market tops before that took years to arrive, if they arrived at all. But his positioning adds a data point to a growing list of credit-market signals — widening spreads on AI-linked debt, scrutiny of vendor-financing arrangements between chipmakers and cloud providers — that suggest not everyone financing the AI buildout is convinced the economics close. The next test comes from the credit market itself: if spreads on freshly issued AI-sector bonds keep widening rather than settling after issuance, that would lend more weight to Gundlach's argument than any single interview can.

diageo-whisky-strike.headline: Diageo's Johnnie Walker and Bell's whisky supplies hit by worker walkout
diageo-whisky-strike.body_md:
Diageo's Scottish supply chain is about to run into a wall of picket lines just as the group closes out its third quarter. More than 100 Unite members at the Cameronbridge distillery in Fife will walk out on Monday 28 September, the start of a rolling three-week stoppage running to 15 October, in a dispute over roughly 10 job cuts at a site that makes the grain-whisky base for Johnnie Walker and Bell's.

> "There is no justification for slashing hundreds of jobs across its operations when it is raking in hundreds of millions of profit."

That's Unite's line on Diageo, and it is not a small claim to level at a company that also insists it needs to cut. Cameronbridge — Europe's largest grain distillery, and by Diageo's own description the birthplace of Cameron Brig — employs around 200 people, with roughly 70 roles under review. It supplies not just Johnnie Walker and Bell's but J&B, Vat 69, White Horse, Black & White and Haig Club, plus the neutral spirit behind Smirnoff, Gordon's and Tanqueray.

![Cameron Bridge Distillery in Fife, Scotland](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Cameron_Bridge_Distillery_-_geograph.org.uk_-_96523.jpg)

## A dispute rooted in a $1bn overhaul

The walkout is the sharpest local flashpoint yet in Diageo's group-wide restructuring, a $1bn cost programme under which the company has already trimmed headcount by around 2,000 globally. Diageo Scotland's after-tax profit fell to £595m in 2025 from £736m the year before — a decline management points to as the rationale for the cuts, and one Unite points to as evidence the reductions are unnecessary. The company's position, delivered through a spokesperson, was blunt: "We are disappointed by the decision to strike. The proposal to remove up to 10 roles at Cameronbridge Distillery is necessary as we maintain reduced production volumes to protect the long-term competitiveness of our business."

Unite's industrial officer Dougie Orchardson takes the opposite view of what happens next: "Industrial action will inevitably result in supply shortages of many people's favourite drinks." Diageo disagrees. Asked directly, a spokesperson said: "We do not envisage any supply shortages," citing contingency planning to keep bottling lines fed through the stoppage.

## Timing that bites

Whichever side is right about shortages, the timing is awkward. The strike dates fall squarely across the final weeks of Diageo's fiscal third quarter, and Johnnie Walker is one of the group's highest-margin brands — the kind of volume that shows up quickly in scotch shipment data if a distillery goes quiet for even part of three weeks. Cameronbridge does not bottle the finished product, but it supplies the grain spirit that blenders need on a schedule; a three-week interruption to that upstream flow is the sort of thing that shows up downstream weeks later, not immediately, which is exactly why analysts will be watching Diageo's next trading update rather than this week's headlines for the real answer.

For now, the numbers in dispute are small next to Diageo's scale — 10 jobs, 100 picketing workers, one Scottish site among dozens of Diageo facilities worldwide. What makes it worth watching is the overlap of a live industrial dispute with a restructuring programme still finding its edges, and a spirits maker that has already told the market its margins are under pressure. The next marker is 28 September, when the first pickets go up; after that, whether Diageo's contingency planning holds through to 15 October will say more about the group's operational resilience than either side's public statements do today.

nato-rutte-defence-spending.headline: NATO's Rutte presses PM Burnham for a 'credible path' to 3.5% GDP defence spending
nato-rutte-defence-spending.body_md:
NATO's secretary-general left Downing Street this week with praise for Andy Burnham's rhetoric and a pointed demand attached to it: show the money, and show it every year, not just at the finish line.

Mark Rutte met the prime minister on Wednesday, then Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting on Thursday, in a two-day visit meant to test how firmly Britain's new government stands behind the target NATO leaders set at The Hague last summer — 3.5% of GDP on core military spending by 2035, with a further 1.5% on broader security and resilience costs on top. "I'm really happy with the Prime Minister... really committing to the 3.5%," Rutte told the Press Association afterwards, "but also committing to the need for a credible path to get there." Then the line that mattered more than the praise: "You cannot spend it today, but you can also not wait 'til 2035. And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments."

It is a small phrase — *yearly increments* — but it is doing a lot of work. NATO has learned, over successive summits, that a distant deadline without intermediate checkpoints is an invitation to defer. Rutte is trying to close that loophole before Britain, or anyone else, opens it.

## The gap between the pledge and the plan

Britain's actual commitment on paper stops well short of the 2035 target. The government has budgeted to raise defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28 — itself an acceleration on the 2.5% pathway set under the previous government — but has published nothing describing how it gets from there to 3.5% over the following seven years. Burnham's government has said only that the fuller trajectory will be set out at next year's spending review.

![NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9b/Mark_Rutte%2C_23.03.23_%28cropped%29.jpg)

That gap is not accidental. It is the residue of a fight that already claimed one Cabinet career. John Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, under Keir Starmer, telling his prime minister that the financial settlement behind the government's own Defence Investment Plan fell well short of what the country needed and accusing the Treasury of being "unwilling" to commit the resources required. Healey is now Chancellor under Burnham — which means the man who quit demanding more defence money now sits on the side of the table that has to find it, a reversal that has not gone unnoticed in Westminster.

Rutte's framing — 50% of Russia's state budget now goes on defence, he has noted repeatedly — is meant to make the arithmetic feel less like an accounting exercise and more like a deterrence problem. "Let's not be naive about what he might do against NATO," he said of Vladimir Putin during the visit. The alliance's institutional memory of Ukraine, and of allies who spent the 2010s hollowing out their militaries on the assumption peace was permanent, sits behind every push for firmer numbers.

## Burnham's domestic bind

The difficulty for Burnham is that the 3.5% question does not arrive in isolation — it lands on top of a government already fighting over where the money for anything comes from. At Prime Minister's Questions this week, pressed by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch on whether the UK would hit 3% of GDP by 2030, Burnham refused to commit to the interim figure and instead drew a different line: "We do everything to support national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security... This side of the house will not be forced to choose between the two, and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

![Andy Burnham](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Official_portrait_of_Andy_Burnham_MP_2026_%28cropped_3x4%29.jpg)

Badenoch had suggested the money could come from housing benefit; Conservative officials accused Burnham of "prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security." Burnham's own line is narrower than a flat refusal to trim welfare — he has previously said he wants to "get the welfare bill down" through measures aimed at young people out of work or training, rather than the disability-payment cuts that Starmer's government tried and failed to push through. But the political signal is unmistakable: this prime minister is not going to fund NATO's target by squeezing the benefits system, which leaves tax rises, borrowing, or slower delivery as the remaining levers — none of them costless with Reform UK holding a commanding poll lead and gilt yields already sitting near three-decade highs.

## What The Hague actually requires

The target itself is less simple than "3.5% of GDP" suggests. The Hague Summit Declaration, agreed by NATO leaders in June 2025 in the alliance's shortest final communiqué in decades, set a two-tier formula: 3.5% of GDP on core military expenditure — personnel, equipment, operations — and a further 1.5% on broader security-related spending such as cyberdefence, critical infrastructure and industrial capacity, for a nominal 5% headline figure that was the price of securing Donald Trump's continued commitment to the alliance. Every member bar Spain, which secured an exemption and committed instead to 2.1%, signed on. National roadmaps were due by the middle of this year; a collective progress review is scheduled for 2029, with 2035 as the hard deadline. There is no enforcement mechanism beyond diplomatic pressure and, implicitly, Washington's patience.

That absence of teeth is precisely why Rutte is leaning so hard on process rather than just outcome. A country that commits to 3.5% by 2035 but back-loads every increase to the final two years is, in practical terms, no different from a country that never committed at all — and NATO's planners cannot build force structures around a number that might arrive all at once in 2034. Yearly increments make the pledge auditable.

Britain's own roadmap, promised for next year's spending review, will be the first real test of whether Burnham's government treats that distinction as binding or as another deadline to be managed. The 2029 alliance-wide review will be the next external checkpoint after that — but for a government already navigating a leadership transition, a restless backbench and a Chancellor who once resigned over exactly this dispute, the more immediate pressure point is domestic: the spending review itself, whenever in the coming months it lands.

uk-eu-defence-fund-access.headline: Chancellor to press EU finance ministers on UK access to joint defence-industry fund
uk-eu-defence-fund-access.body_md:
John Healey spent Thursday in Dublin doing something his predecessor at the Treasury tried and abandoned: asking the European Union to let Britain into its flagship defence-industrial financing scheme. The Chancellor raised the UK's case for access to the Security Action for Europe fund — SAFE, the EU's €150bn loan facility for joint military procurement — on the sidelines of the informal ECOFIN meeting hosted by Ireland's Tánaiste and finance minister, Simon Harris, as part of Dublin's EU Council presidency.

It is, on its face, a rerun. Rachel Reeves's Treasury negotiated over SAFE membership through much of 2025 and walked away in December, after the European Commission and France pushed for an entry fee of up to €6bn — a figure Yvette Cooper, then at the Foreign Office, said failed the government's own "value for money" test. Canada, by contrast, secured its SAFE association agreement for a reported €10m, a gap of more than 500-to-1 that UK officials called indefensible and MPs on the Commons foreign affairs committee queried directly with ministers.

## Same fund, different pitch

What has changed since December is less the fund's terms than the Treasury occupant making the case. Healey took over from Reeves in Andy Burnham's first reshuffle on 20 July, arriving from the Ministry of Defence with a working relationship with EU counterparts built over eighteen months of Ukraine-related procurement talks. His pitch in Dublin leans on geopolitics rather than accountancy: a Europe rearming against Russia, an unpredictable US security guarantee under Trump, and a UK defence industry that argues exclusion from SAFE-funded joint procurement locks British suppliers out of contracts EU rivals can bid for freely.

The financial argument runs through the City. SAFE loans are raised by the Commission on capital markets against the EU's balance sheet and then lent on to member states — a pipeline of debt issuance, structuring and advisory work that UK banks want a share of, much as they lobbied for a foothold in the EU's post-2020 pandemic recovery bonds. Treasury officials frame renewed SAFE access as a way of keeping London-based underwriting inside the tent rather than watching Frankfurt and Paris capture the mandates.

## A crowded field of defence banks

Complicating the pitch is that Healey is simultaneously exploring alternatives to SAFE rather than relying on it alone. The UK has been building a Multilateral Defence Mechanism with the Netherlands, Finland and Poland — sovereign-governed, unlike SAFE's Commission-run allocation — and is weighing membership of the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, backed by JPMorgan, RBC, Commerzbank, ING and LBBW. Reeves rejected the DSRB idea when it was first floated; Healey has reopened that file too, according to people briefed on the talks. Reconciling overlapping memberships across three defence-financing tracks — one EU-run, one UK-led, one transatlantic — is now as much a diplomatic exercise as a financial one.

Dublin's talks continue into Saturday, with a press conference expected to close the informal session, though no SAFE decision is likely this week — Brussels typically takes such requests through full Council process. The clearer marker to watch is the spring UK spending review, where Healey has promised to lay out, for the first time, a costed path to the NATO target of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. Whatever SAFE access looks like by then will shape how much of that spending flows through EU-run channels rather than British or transatlantic ones — and how much of the underwriting fee income lands in London.

reform-uk-poll-lead.headline: Reform UK holds strong poll lead as Burnham's Labour struggles to stabilise
reform-uk-poll-lead.body_md:
Andy Burnham has been prime minister for exactly nine weeks, and the polling verdict on his premiership so far is: not disastrous, but not the recovery Labour needed either.

The latest PollCheck seven-poll moving average, updated 17 September, puts Labour on 25.4% against Reform UK's 23.3% — a lead of barely two points, well inside a general sense of statistical noise. YouGov's most recent voting-intention poll, fielded 13-14 September, has the two parties tied at 23% apiece. Other pollsters tell a different story: Ipsos fieldwork earlier this year had Reform ahead by anywhere from two to eight points. Which party is "winning" now depends almost entirely on which house's methodology a reader trusts — an unusual state of affairs for a governing party that spent the past year trailing by double digits.

## A weak start, then a weaker one

Burnham's personal numbers explain why nobody in government is celebrating the tightened race. His first Ipsos satisfaction rating after taking office in July — 29% satisfied — was worse than Keir Starmer's first reading as PM (37%), and nowhere close to Theresa May (54%), David Cameron (57%) or Tony Blair (65%) at the equivalent point in their premierships. It was, in other words, one of the weakest opening satisfaction scores Ipsos has recorded for an incoming prime minister.

The trend since hasn't reversed it. YouGov's September favourability tracker shows Burnham's unfavourable rating climbing six points to 39% — the highest since he entered Downing Street — even as his favourable rating held flat at 46%. Ipsos's own job-satisfaction question, a stricter measure, now finds only around three in ten Britons satisfied with his performance, with roughly four in ten saying they simply don't know.

![Andy Burnham's official portrait as Prime Minister, taken at 10 Downing Street in July 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Chancellor John Healey fares no better. YouGov puts his favourability at 16%, unchanged since August, while his unfavourable share has risen five points to 24% — and six in ten voters still have no opinion of him at all, a sign the Treasury has yet to make much of an impression either way. Ipsos separately puts overall government satisfaction at just 18%, against roughly seven in ten dissatisfied.

## Why it matters for markets

None of this amounts to a crisis signal on its own — a two-point polling gap is not a mandate crisis, and Burnham's net favourability, while sliding, remains positive by the standards of recent premierships. But a government with thin personal capital and a razor-thin lead over an insurgent opposition has less room to spend on unpopular fiscal choices, whether that's the tax rises needed to fund the defence-spending path NATO's Mark Rutte has been pressing for, or further gilt issuance at yields already sitting near three-decade highs. Sterling and gilts have so far shrugged off the polling noise, largely because no single pollster commands consensus and no election is imminent. That calculus changes quickly if the averages converge on a clear Reform lead.

The next test is due before month-end, when Ipsos and YouGov both refresh their trackers; a by-election in Makerfield, watched closely inside Downing Street as a proxy for Burnham's personal standing, will offer the first real-world check on whether the polling divergence reflects genuine volatility or just sampling noise.

un-war-crimes-iran-strikes.headline: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in strikes on Iran
un-war-crimes-iran-strikes.body_md:
Nearly seven months after the war between the United States and Iran opened with one of the most concentrated decapitation strikes in modern military history, the conflict has acquired a new and awkward dimension: a formal international finding that the strikes themselves may have broken the laws of war.

An independent panel of investigators appointed by the UN Human Rights Council said on Thursday it had found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two of the airstrikes that opened the war on 28 February — attacks the mission says killed at least 178 civilians, including roughly 120 children, at a school and a sports complex hundreds of miles from the military and leadership targets the opening barrage was designed to destroy.

![Human Rights and Alliance of Civilizations Room, the Geneva chamber where the UN Human Rights Council meets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/UN_Geneva_Human_Rights_and_Alliance_of_Civilizations_Room.jpg)

## What the mission found

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, chaired by the Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and created by the Human Rights Council in 2022, examined two strikes carried out on the war's opening day. One used Tomahawk cruise missiles against the Tree of Tayyiba Elementary School in Minab, in Iran's south, killing more than 150 people. The other struck a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd using precision munitions that dispersed tungsten pellets over a wide radius, killing 22 more.

The investigators concluded the school was not collateral damage from a strike on a nearby Revolutionary Guard facility but the intended point of impact — despite what the report describes as unmistakable markers of civilian use, including "child-oriented murals painted on exterior walls, school signage, and playground areas." Their finding: the US had failed "to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective," meeting the legal threshold for the war crime of an indiscriminate attack.

![A Tomahawk cruise missile launches from a US Navy destroyer](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/59/US_Navy_090825-N-1522S-020_A_Tactical_Tomahawk_Cruise_Missile_launches_from_the_forward_missile_deck_aboard_the_guided-missile_destroyer_USS_Farragut_%28DDG_99%29_during_a_training_exercise.jpg)

Those two strikes were a small part of a far larger operation. In the opening minutes of the war, US and Israeli forces launched close to 900 strikes within twelve hours, aimed squarely at Iran's command structure. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed, along with roughly 40 senior officials — among them the defence minister, the IRGC's overall commander, the head of the Basij paramilitary force, the intelligence minister and the armed forces' chief of staff. Whatever one makes of the legality of targeting a state's top leadership in an active conflict, the mission's war crimes finding is not about that campaign. It concerns two strikes, on the same day, that hit a school and a housing block instead.

## A report with two targets

The mission did not train its findings on Washington alone. The same report accuses Iran's government of crimes against humanity in its crackdown on the protest movement that has run alongside the war since 2025, describing killings by state security forces "on a staggering scale" across every province. Investigators documented at least 221 children killed, tens of thousands held in arbitrary detention with reports of torture and solitary confinement, and at least 29 executions following summary trials, with more than 70 further death sentences pending. Tehran has put its own death toll from the unrest at just over 3,000; the mission suggests the real figure is higher.

That dual indictment matters for how the report lands politically. It gives Washington an obvious rhetorical exit — treat the document as proof of UN even-handedness gone wrong, or dismiss it wholesale. A State Department official did the latter within hours of publication, saying the US does not extend the report credibility and accusing the Human Rights Council of pushing "anti-American rhetoric and antisemitism" that "appeases repressive regimes." The White House has previously and repeatedly denied that the February strikes constituted war crimes.

## Why a non-binding report still counts

The fact-finding mission has no power to prosecute anyone. Its report is a recommendation to the Human Rights Council, not a verdict, and the United States is not a member of the International Criminal Court, which limits the avenues by which any of this could turn into an actual case. But documents like this rarely die where they're published. They build an evidentiary record — witness testimony, satellite imagery, munitions analysis — that other courts, truth commissions or future administrations can draw on years later, the same function similar UN mechanisms have served for Syria and the occupied Palestinian territories.

More immediately, the finding narrows the diplomatic space available to end a war that, per [Iran war ceasefire still fraying past the 200-day mark](/iran-ceasefire-frays), has already produced a ceasefire in name only. A negotiated settlement typically requires both sides to accept some version of amnesty or forbearance on past conduct; a formal war-crimes determination against one party makes that harder to sell domestically, on either side. It also adds a legal frame to a conflict that financial markets have mostly been pricing as a supply-side oil shock — a dynamic visible in the [surge past $100 a barrel](/oil-tops-100-saudi-pipeline) after pipeline attacks disrupted Saudi and regional exports.

The mission's report goes to the Human Rights Council for formal presentation in the coming weeks, where member states will debate a response that could range from a strongly worded resolution to nothing at all — the Council has no enforcement power of its own. The more consequential test is whether any government or court with actual jurisdiction picks up the evidentiary trail the mission has laid down. Until then, the war grinds on largely as before, with one more entry on the growing list of grievances neither side is likely to forget at the negotiating table.
